presenceLabel: Green River Archaic area (archaeological culture, not a tribe)
presenceNote: An archaeological culture, not a tribe: a group of shell-midden sites in west-central Kentucky that archaeologists define from the tools, shell heaps and dates they share. About 4000–1000 BCE (6,000 to 3,000 years ago). Drawn: five whole counties (Butler, Ohio, Henderson, McLean, Muhlenberg) where more than 1,700 prehistoric sites are recorded. A general area, not a boundary; no site locations are shown. Medium confidence (years high, area medium).
overlapNote: Later Woodland, Fort Ancient-era and Mississippian people used some of the same shell middens, and Henderson County also lies in the later Caborn-Welborn area (about 1400–1700); those are other times, so the year slider keeps them apart. No mapped nation overlaps this time.
basis: Kentucky Archaeological Survey / Kentucky Heritage Council education booklet (2006) and the National Register nomination for the Green River shell middens. Public agency sources.

eras.label: 4000–1000 BCE · Green River Archaic shell-midden sites
eras.text: The Green River Archaic is an archaeological culture, a group of sites that archaeologists define from the tools, shell heaps and dates they share; it is not a tribe, and no descent from or link to any later people is claimed. According to the Kentucky Archaeological Survey, its way of life flourished between 4,000 and 1,000 BC (6,000 to 3,000 years ago), and archaeologists have recorded more than 1,700 prehistoric sites in Butler, Ohio, Henderson, McLean and Muhlenberg counties, many with deep heaps of freshwater mussel shell. The tint is those five whole counties: a general area, not a boundary. The booklet counts sites by county and draws no edge, and exact site locations are kept confidential, so none are shown. The sites overlap in place, not in time, with much later camps and villages.
